q: State the function of the urinary bladder.

pts.a: Stores urine (until it is released through the urethra)
accept: holds urine until it is released

right: It stores urine until it is released through the urethra.
wrong: It makes urine by filtering the blood
It carries urine out of the body
It reabsorbs water from the urine
why: The kidneys make urine all the time. The bladder holds it, so it can be released at a suitable time instead of trickling out constantly.

q: Explain how urine is moved along the ureter to the bladder.

pts.a: Peristalsis: waves of contraction of the muscle in the ureter wall
accept: muscles in the ureter wall contract in waves
the muscle squeezes the urine along

right: By peristalsis: waves of contraction of the muscle in the ureter wall.
wrong: It is pumped there by the blood pressure from the heart
By cilia that sweep the urine along the tube
By osmosis through the wall of the ureter
why: Smooth muscle in the ureter wall contracts in waves (peristalsis), pushing urine down to the bladder, even when you are lying down.

q: Give one feature of the wall of the urinary bladder that suits it to its function.

pts.a: Elastic (stretchy) wall, so it expands as urine collects
Muscular wall that contracts to push urine out
accept: muscle in the wall squeezes the urine out

right: Its wall is elastic, so it can stretch as it fills with urine.
wrong: It has microvilli to give a large surface area
Its wall is one cell thick for fast diffusion
It is surrounded by capillaries to reabsorb water
why: The bladder wall stretches as urine collects, so it can hold a lot, and its muscle contracts to push the urine out through the urethra.

q: Name the part of the nephron where all the glucose is reabsorbed into the blood.

pts.a: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)

wrong: The loop of Henle
The collecting duct
The distal convoluted tubule
why: Everything useful comes back in the PCT, the first stretch after Bowman's capsule. The loop of Henle and DCT take back water and salts.

q: State how glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.

pts.a: Active transport

right: By active transport, which uses energy from ATP.
wrong: By osmosis, along with the water
By diffusion, with no energy used
By filtration under high pressure
why: Glucose is pumped back into the blood against its concentration gradient so that none is lost in urine. This needs energy: active transport.

q: Give two ways the cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule are adapted for reabsorption.

pts.a: Microvilli (for a large surface area)
accept: folded membrane for a large surface area

pts.a: Many mitochondria (energy for active transport)
Close to many capillaries or lining one cell thick (short distance)
accept: the lining is one cell thick

right: Microvilli give a large surface area; many mitochondria supply energy.
wrong: They have cilia to sweep the filtrate along
They have thick walls and store glycogen
They are impermeable to water and have no nucleus
why: Microvilli give a large surface area to take substances back, and many mitochondria make the ATP needed for active transport.

q: Explain how water is reabsorbed from the loop of Henle.

pts.a: By osmosis
The surrounding medulla is very salty (high salt concentration)
accept: the medulla has a high salt concentration
salts are pumped out into the medulla
the tissue fluid around it is very salty

right: By osmosis, because the medulla around the loop is very salty.
wrong: By active transport, using energy from ATP
By filtration, as the blood pressure is high
By diffusion of salts into the blood
why: Salts pumped out of the ascending limb make the medulla very salty, so water leaves the descending limb by osmosis and returns to the blood.

q: Explain why the cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria.

pts.a: To release energy (ATP) for active transport (of glucose and amino acids)
accept: to make ATP for active transport

right: To release energy (ATP) for the active transport of glucose.
wrong: To make urea from spare amino acids
To give a large surface area for diffusion
To store the glucose that is reabsorbed
why: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, making ATP. Taking glucose and amino acids back by active transport uses a lot of ATP.

q: Explain why glucose must be reabsorbed by active transport rather than by diffusion.

pts.a: Glucose moves against its concentration gradient (from low to high concentration)
accept: it moves against the concentration gradient

pts.a: So that all the glucose is reabsorbed and none is lost in urine
accept: so none of the glucose is lost in the urine
so that all the glucose is taken back

right: It moves against its concentration gradient, so all of it is taken back.
wrong: Glucose molecules are too large to diffuse through a membrane
Diffusion only works for gases like oxygen
Active transport needs no energy, so it is cheaper
why: Diffusion would stop once the filtrate and blood had equal glucose levels, so some would be lost. Active transport pumps it all back, against the gradient.

q: Other than water, name a substance reabsorbed from the loop of Henle.

pts.a: Salts (or named, e.g. sodium chloride, sodium ions) or minerals

wrong: Glucose, by active transport
Amino acids
Plasma proteins
why: Salts are pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla. Glucose and amino acids were all taken back earlier, in the PCT.

pts.a: The control of the water and salt balance (concentration) of the body
accept: regulating the water and salt content of the blood
keeping the water and salt concentration of body fluids constant
maintaining the water balance and salt balance

right: The control of the water and salt balance of the body.
wrong: The control of body temperature by sweating
The movement of water across a membrane by osmosis
The removal of the waste products of metabolism
why: Osmoregulation is part of homeostasis: the kidneys, guided by ADH, keep the water and salt concentration of the blood steady.

q: Name the organ that carries out osmoregulation in humans and the hormone that controls it.

pts.a: Kidney
ADH (anti-diuretic hormone, vasopressin)

right: The kidney, controlled by the hormone ADH.
wrong: The liver, controlled by the hormone insulin
The skin, controlled by the hormone adrenaline
The kidney, controlled by the hormone thyroxine
why: The kidneys control how much water and salt leave in urine. ADH, released by the pituitary gland, sets how much water they take back.

q: Explain why osmoregulation is important for the cells of the body.

pts.a: Stops cells gaining or losing too much water by osmosis (so they do not burst or shrink)
accept: so cells do not burst or shrivel
so the cells do not lose or gain too much water by osmosis
so that cells don't swell up

right: So cells do not gain or lose too much water by osmosis and burst or shrink.
wrong: So that cells can make urea for excretion
So enzymes in the cells are not denatured by heat
So that cells get enough glucose for respiration
why: If body fluids are too dilute, cells take in water by osmosis and swell; if too concentrated, they lose water and shrink. Either way they stop working well.

q: Name two substances in the blood whose levels are controlled by osmoregulation.

pts.a: Water
Salts (or named, e.g. sodium chloride) or ions

right: Water and salts, such as sodium chloride.
wrong: Glucose and insulin
Oxygen and carbon dioxide
Urea and amino acids
why: Osmo- means water pressure: osmoregulation balances water against dissolved salts. Glucose is controlled by insulin, and gases by breathing.

q: State the effect of drinking a large volume of water on the amount of ADH released.

pts.a: Less ADH is released (by the pituitary gland)

right: Less ADH is released by the pituitary gland.
wrong: More ADH is released to remove the extra water
The kidneys release ADH instead of the pituitary
The amount of ADH stays the same
why: Extra water makes the blood too dilute. So the pituitary gland releases less ADH and the kidneys keep back less water.

q: Explain how a low level of ADH affects the reabsorption of water in the collecting ducts.

pts.a: The walls (of the collecting duct and DCT) become less permeable to water
accept: the collecting duct becomes impermeable to water

pts.a: Less water is reabsorbed (into the blood)
accept: more water stays in the tubule
less water goes back into the blood

right: The walls become less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed.
wrong: The walls become more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed
The walls actively pump glucose back into the blood
The walls become thicker, so more salt is filtered
why: ADH opens the collecting duct walls to water. With little ADH they stay closed to it, so less water is taken back and more stays in the urine.

q: State the effect on the urine of drinking a lot of water.

pts.a: A large volume of urine
Dilute urine

right: A large volume of dilute urine is produced.
wrong: A small volume of concentrated urine is produced
The urine contains glucose and protein
No change, as the extra water is stored in the bladder
why: With less ADH, less water is taken back in the collecting ducts, so the extra water leaves as lots of dilute urine and the blood returns to normal.

q: Explain why the control of ADH release is an example of negative feedback.

pts.a: The response reverses (cancels) the change, bringing the blood back to normal
accept: it brings the water concentration back to normal
the effect is opposite to the change

right: The response reverses the change, so the blood's water level returns to normal.
wrong: The response makes the change bigger and bigger
ADH is released by a gland, not by a nerve
Less ADH is made when there is less glucose in the blood
why: In negative feedback the response cancels the change: dilute blood means less ADH, so more water leaves in urine until the blood is back to normal.
